```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)
library(simCoDaR)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggdist)
```

The fitted simulator learns a **joint distribution of selected assay
logratios**, not just a set of independent proportions that sum to one.
You can generate synthetic subcompositions to test how statistical methods
respond to observed multivariate dependence. This is a statistical model
of an assay dataset, not an inference of mineralogy, texture, recovery,
spatial continuity, or deposit-scale physical calibration.

If you need **known mineralogical truth and theoretical assay chemistry**,
start instead with the [commodity scenario vignette](commodity-scenarios.html).
That workflow begins with explicit, uncalibrated mineral mixtures.

## Choose the simulation workflow

| Starting information | Generate | What it does **not** establish |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Hypothetical mineral fractions and domain targets | Closed mineral compositions, then ideal element/oxide reporting | A fitted deposit model or measured XRD/XRF/ICP response |
| Measured assays with compatible, nonoverlapping parts | New draws from a fitted joint compositional distribution | Mineral phase truth, original assay total or spatial continuity |

These workflows are **not yet a joint calibrated mineralogy-to-assay model**.
In particular, fitting oxide ratios cannot recover their contributing mineral
phases: multiple mineral mixtures can produce similar bulk chemistry.

## Select a common measurement basis

The installed example comes from Zindorf, März and Schnetger (2020),
[Site U1418, IODP Expedition 341](https://doi.org/10.2204/iodp.proc.341.206.2020).
Major oxides are dry-sediment **wt%**; separate trace columns are **ppm** and depth
is **m CCSF-A**. This sediment core illustrates statistical fitting, not an ore
calibration population. The authors' data are CC BY 4.0; package code is GPL-3.
The bundled CSV selects and renames workbook columns without changing numerical
cells or blanks. It has 284 identified rows; the report says 285 analysed.
The workbook checksum is historical, with no fresh cell-equivalence claim.

```{r data}
assays <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "iodp_u1418_major_trace.csv",
                             package = "simCoDaR", mustWork = TRUE),
                   check.names = FALSE) %>% as_tibble()
parts <- c("SiO2", "TiO2", "Al2O3", "Fe2O3", "MnO", "MgO", "CaO",
           "Na2O", "K2O", "P2O5")
assays %>% summarise(rows = n(), unique_samples = n_distinct(sample_id),
                    reported_total_min = min(oxide_total_wt_pct),
                    reported_total_max = max(oxide_total_wt_pct))
```

All ten selected oxides are positive. Reported totals range from 90.8 to 96.2
wt%; we retain those amounts in the source table. Fitting closes only the selected
parts: each is divided by their row sum. Outputs are fractions of that selected
sum, not recovered dry-sediment wt%. No remainder or total-to-100 correction is
created. Trace ppm, elemental equivalents and mineral volume percentages must
not be mixed into this closure. Unit labels describe inputs and never convert
them; the caller must establish nonoverlapping chemical species.

## Freeze the holdout before fitting

Choose a 71-row contiguous interval in depth order using a declared RNG and seed.
All four families use its same 213-row complement in original row order.
Depth influences the split only. No heldout observations choose parameters,
mixture size, degrees of freedom or transformations.

```{r split}
scoped <- function(seed, code) withr::with_seed(seed, code,
  .rng_kind = "Mersenne-Twister", .rng_normal_kind = "Inversion",
  .rng_sample_kind = "Rejection")
ordered <- order(assays$depth_m, seq_len(nrow(assays)))
start <- scoped(20260924L, sample.int(214L, 1L))
heldout_rows <- sort(ordered[seq.int(start, length.out = 71L)])
training_rows <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(assays)), heldout_rows)
train <- assays[training_rows, ]
heldout <- assays[heldout_rows, ]
tibble(training_n = nrow(train), heldout_n = nrow(heldout), start = start,
       depth_min = min(heldout$depth_m), depth_max = max(heldout$depth_m))
models <- c("dirichlet", "logistic_normal", "ilr_student_t", "ilr_mixture")
```

With this RNG, start is 108 and the interval is 298.470–539.290 m CCSF-A.
The historical exact primary interval and RNG environment are unavailable;
this is a new reproduction of the recovered recipe. Nearby core rows are
correlated, so heldout performance is a depth sensitivity check rather than
independent geological external validation.

## Fit once, then draw

Dirichlet uses positive-alpha maximum likelihood. It is a restricted baseline:
distinct-part population covariance is always negative. Logistic normal fits
full covariance in nine orthonormal logratio (ILR) dimensions. Student t fits
location and full **scale** at predeclared df5; its covariance is 5/3 times scale.
The mixture fits full component covariance with multiple starts, choosing k2 or
k3 by **training BIC**. Statistical components do not identify geological facies.
Inspect convergence, failed candidates and regularization before interpreting a fit.

```{r fit}
fits <- set_names(models) %>% map(function(model) {
  scoped(20260924L, fit_assay_simulator(train, parts, model,
    seed = 20260924L, student_df = 5, mixture_components = 2:3,
    unit_label = "wt%", measurement_basis = "oxide_mass"))
})
# Public fit objects expose parameters and diagnostics; no private helpers.
pattern <- fits$ilr_mixture$groups[[1]]$patterns[[1]]
tibble(k = as.integer(names(pattern$model$bic)),
       training_BIC = as.numeric(pattern$model$bic))
pattern$model$selected_components
pattern$model$diagnostics
synthetic <- scoped(123L, simulate_assays(fits$ilr_student_t, n = 71, seed = 123L))
synthetic %>% summarise(across(all_of(parts), mean))
attr(synthetic, "diagnostics")
```

### Inspect generated proportions

```{r generated-proportions}
# The generated rows sum to one across the selected oxide parts.
stopifnot(max(abs(rowSums(synthetic[parts]) - 1)) < 1e-10)

# A single synthetic draw has a descriptive, not guaranteed, correlation.
round(cor(synthetic[c("Fe2O3", "MgO")]), 3)
```

Multiplying a simulated value by 100 yields **percent of the selected
ten-oxide sum**, not the corresponding whole-rock oxide wt%. Recovering
absolute wt% would require an explicitly fitted or specified total model,
which this API does not provide. Neither closure nor a favourable
correlation from one draw proves the model reproduces real geology.

`fit_assay_simulator()` returns a serializable `geo_assay_simulator` list with
part order, fitted basis, parameters, aggregate counts, controls, assumptions and
RNG/version metadata. It omits training rows/IDs/totals; parameters and necessary
group labels can still disclose information. `simulate_assays()` returns a data
frame of closed fractions with assumptions and diagnostics attributes. Sparse
supports and nonconvergence fail explicitly, without resampling raw rows.
Zeros are refused by default. Only metadata-established structural absence may
be declared; censoring, rounding and missing values need a separate model.
Grouped/structural fitting is available, but the first public validator supports
only positive, ungrouped full support. No total or total–composition model is fitted.

## Compare heldout distributions

The laptop tutorial uses four primary fits and **four 71-row draws per model**.
It does not rerun the complete five-split study. All log scores use the same fitted
ordered Helmert ILR Lebesgue measure. For Dirichlet the coordinate-simplex density
is converted by subtracting log J, where log J = −log(D)/2 − sum(log x).
Comparing unadjusted simplex and ILR densities would give misleading scores.
Higher mean log score is better; lower energy, covariance error and logratio
quantile discrepancy are better, but these assess different aspects.

```{r diagnose}
evaluations <- imap(fits, function(fit, model) {
  m <- match(model, models)
  base_seed <- 20261014L + 100L * m
  scoped(base_seed, validate_assay_simulator(fit, heldout, reference = train,
    n_draws = 71L, replicates = 4L, seed = base_seed))
})
score_table <- imap_dfr(evaluations, function(x, model) {
  tibble(model = model, mean_ILR_log_score = x$score_summary$mean_log_score,
         draw_failures = nrow(x$failures))
})
score_table %>% arrange(desc(mean_ILR_log_score))
metrics <- imap_dfr(evaluations, function(x, model) {
  as_tibble(x$mc_summary) %>% mutate(model = model, .before = 1)
})
metrics %>% filter(metric %in% c("ilr_energy", "ilr_covariance_relative_error",
                                "mean_absolute_logratio_quantile_error"), statistic == "generated")
```

Energy is the ILR V-statistic including diagonal zero distances. Covariance error
is relative Frobenius error using sample covariance. Pairwise logratio quantiles
use probabilities .05, .25, .5, .75, .95 (type7). Tail diagnostics use strict
heldout thresholds and, when reference is supplied, training closed-part .01/.99
bounds; the latter count **cells**, not rows. The output retains pointwise scores,
long replicate metrics, generated/discrepancy MC summaries, failure messages and
metadata, rather than input or generated assay tables.

MCSE is sample SD divided by sqrt(successful repetitions): conditional draw
noise given this fit and heldout set. Four repetitions provide a rough tutorial
estimate, not field uncertainty, parameter uncertainty or a confidence interval.
Check success/failure counts; incomplete summaries must not be treated as complete.
The validator never fits or tunes a model and does not certify scientific validity.

## See learned dependence and marginals

Use one fresh 71-row draw per model for display. All panels show **closed selected
oxide percent**, not original wt%. Identical axes allow comparisons with the
heldout relationships. A draw is illustrative; the replicate diagnostics above
are better for quantifying stochastic differences.

```{r plot-data}
close_percent <- function(x) {
  x %>% select(all_of(parts)) %>%
    mutate(total = rowSums(pick(all_of(parts)))) %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(parts), ~ 100 * .x / total)) %>% select(-total)
}
observed <- close_percent(heldout) %>% mutate(distribution = "Heldout")
draws <- imap_dfr(fits, function(fit, model) {
  scoped(20262014L + match(model, models),
    simulate_assays(fit, 71L, seed = 20262014L + match(model, models))) %>%
    as_tibble() %>% mutate(across(all_of(parts), ~ 100 * .x), distribution = model)
})
plot_data <- bind_rows(observed, draws) %>%
  mutate(distribution = factor(distribution, levels = c("Heldout", models)))
relationship <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(Fe2O3, MgO)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .65, size = 1.4, colour = "#25666d") +
  facet_wrap(~ distribution, ncol = 3) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "Fe2O3–MgO dependence in the selected oxide subcomposition",
       subtitle = "71 untouched heldout rows; one illustrative draw per fitted family",
       x = "Closed Fe2O3 (% of ten-oxide sum)",
       y = "Closed MgO (% of ten-oxide sum)")
relationship
```

```{r rainclouds, fig.height=6}
marginals <- plot_data %>% select(distribution, Fe2O3, MgO) %>%
  pivot_longer(-distribution, names_to = "oxide", values_to = "closed_percent")
raincloud <- ggplot(marginals, aes(distribution, closed_percent, fill = distribution)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = .7, width = .6, justification = -.18,
                       point_interval = NULL, .width = 0, alpha = .7) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = .09, height = 0, seed = 20261014L),
             size = .9, alpha = .4) +
  facet_wrap(~ oxide, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#444444", "#a96b39", "#26858c", "#7676a9", "#719340")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "Marginals: heldout assays and fitted draws",
       subtitle = "Half densities and exact-valued points; categorical jitter only",
       x = NULL, y = "Closed selected oxide (%)")
raincloud
```

Half densities are smoothed distributions, not uncertainty bands; widths are
normalized within panels and do not represent counts. Separate marginal panels
cannot establish joint dependence. Dirichlet's distinct-proportion covariance
is −alpha_a alpha_b / [alpha_0²(alpha_0+1)]; positive finite-draw correlation can
occur by chance even though its population restriction cannot match the positive
heldout Fe2O3–MgO relationship.

To save standalone figures after running these chunks, choose a writable output
folder. PNG and SVG use the same ggplot objects; R's SVG device avoids an extra
export dependency:

```{r export, eval=FALSE}
figure_dir <- tempfile("assay-figures-")
dir.create(figure_dir)
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(figure_dir, "relationship.png"), relationship,
               width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 160, bg = "white")
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(figure_dir, "marginals.png"), raincloud,
               width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 160, bg = "white")
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(figure_dir, "relationship.svg"), relationship,
               width = 10, height = 6, device = grDevices::svg, bg = "white")
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(figure_dir, "marginals.svg"), raincloud,
               width = 10, height = 7, device = grDevices::svg, bg = "white")
```

## Using the generated data responsibly

This workflow is useful for checking statistical algorithms under a
measured, fitted dependence structure. It is **not** a source of independent
geological samples: the generated data inherit the selected dataset,
measurement basis, modelling assumptions and any sampling biases.

For method benchmarks, preserve a separate evaluation sample and keep model
selection, transformations and tuning inside training data. The held-out
scores here describe predictive fit to one sediment core, not the accuracy
of mineral proportions or a causal effect.

If your objective is **element-to-mineral conversion**, use the known
mineral-truth simulation from the commodity vignette as a separate test
fixture. Do not treat the ten fitted oxide parts as minerals or pass them
to `minerals_to_assay()`. Connecting observed mineral abundances with
measured assays requires paired data, compatible mass/volume bases and an
explicit measurement/chemistry model.

## Full companion and recorded reproduction

The installed companion freezes all five manifests/configuration before fitting,
then runs 20 fits and 400 small draw tables sequentially. It also reports training
BIC, pointwise scores, candidate/failure diagnostics and paired descriptive
400-bootstrap primary score differences. Running it is optional and separate
from this tutorial:

```{r companion, eval=FALSE}
script <- system.file("examples", "iodp-empirical.R", package = "simCoDaR",
                      mustWork = TRUE)
out <- tempfile("iodp-five-splits-")
system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript"), c(shQuote(script), shQuote(out), "full"))
# Use "freeze" to write manifests only, or "smoke" for one normal fit and tiny draws.
```

The recorded new reproduction used 20 draws per model/split. Student t had highest
log score and Dirichlet lowest on all five splits. Primary mean ILR log scores
were 7.352454, 16.055868, 17.381956 and 16.556801 in the model order above.
Primary energy (mean ± conditional MCSE) was Dirichlet 0.138366 ± 0.003432,
normal 0.012168 ± 0.000658, Student 0.011937 ± 0.001036 and mixture
0.011680 ± 0.001015. The historical primary normal-better-energy claim was not
reproduced; normal energy was lower than Student on the four additional folds.
Differences in split/RNG and convergence methods preclude exact historical
numerical recovery. These ranks are observed results, never code acceptance
criteria. The paired iid bootstrap is descriptive because it ignores depth dependence.

Primary heldout closed Fe2O3–MgO correlation was 0.808654. Mean generated
correlations were −0.061960, 0.879018, 0.874369 and 0.871385. All mixtures
selected k2 on training BIC; recorded fits/draws had no failures or inverse floors.
Inspect actual diagnostics in every new use; this is not a universal guarantee.
Additional heldout depth ranges are 1.434–214.346, 216.368–414.250,
421.390–667.370 and 673.610–972.210 m; their training sets overlap.
